title: Finite fields and Frobenius
subject: finite-fields
summary: Every finite field has a unique extension of each degree, up to isomorphism. Frobenius determines conjugates, subfields, and factor degrees.
questionsAnswered: How does Frobenius determine conjugates and subfields?
How does an irreducible polynomial factor over a larger finite field?
How do trace, norm, and root order determine polynomial coefficients and degrees?

sections.title: Fields from irreducible polynomials
sections.body:
Let \(q=p^r\), where \(p\) is prime. A finite field with \(q\) elements is denoted by \(\mathbb F_q\). Its characteristic is \(p\); as a vector space over \(\mathbb F_p\), it has dimension \(r\).

If \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) is monic and irreducible of degree \(n\), then \[K=\mathbb F_q[x]/(f)\] is a field with \(q^n\) elements. Writing \(\alpha=x\bmod f\), every element has a unique expression \(a_0+a_1\alpha+\cdots+a_{n-1}\alpha^{n-1}\). Addition is coefficientwise; multiplication is followed by reduction modulo \(f\).

Example

The polynomial \(x^2+x+1\) has no root in \(\mathbb F_2\). Thus \(\mathbb F_4=\mathbb F_2(\alpha)\), where \(\alpha^2=\alpha+1\). Its elements are \(0,1,\alpha,\alpha+1\), and \(\alpha^3=1\). The ring \(\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z\) is different: it has characteristic four and is not a field.

sections.title: Existence and uniqueness
sections.body:
In an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb F_q\), the roots of \(x^{q^n}-x\) form a field. Indeed, the identity \((a+b)^{q^n}=a^{q^n}+b^{q^n}\) gives closure under addition, and multiplication and inversion preserve the equation. The derivative is \(-1\), so there are exactly \(q^n\) distinct roots.

Every field with \(q^n\) elements is a splitting field of this polynomial over \(\mathbb F_q\). Uniqueness of splitting fields therefore gives uniqueness up to \(\mathbb F_q\)-isomorphism. We may choose all these fields inside one algebraic closure.

sections.title: Frobenius and conjugates
sections.body:
The map \(\sigma(a)=a^q\) is an automorphism of \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\) fixing \(\mathbb F_q\). It has order \(n\): its \(n\)-th power is the identity, while \(\sigma^j=1\) with \(0

If \(\alpha\) has degree \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\), its conjugates are \(\alpha,\alpha^q,\ldots,\alpha^{q^{d-1}}\). They are distinct, and its minimal polynomial is their product \[m_\alpha(x)=\prod_{i=0}^{d-1}(x-\alpha^{q^i}).\] Frobenius permutes the roots, so the coefficients belong to its fixed field \(\mathbb F_q\).

sections.title: Subfields
sections.body:
There is a subfield \(\mathbb F_{q^d}\subseteq\mathbb F_{q^n}\) exactly when \(d\mid n\), and it is unique. It consists of the elements fixed by \(\sigma^d\). This is the Galois correspondence for the subgroups of a cyclic group.

Inside a fixed algebraic closure, \[\mathbb F_{q^a}\cap\mathbb F_{q^b}=\mathbb F_{q^{\gcd(a,b)}},\qquad \mathbb F_{q^a}\mathbb F_{q^b}=\mathbb F_{q^{\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)}}.\] In particular, an element of \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\) has degree \(n\) if and only if it lies in none of the maximal proper subfields \(\mathbb F_{q^{n/\ell}}\), where \(\ell\) ranges over the prime divisors of \(n\).

sections.title: Changing the field
sections.body:
Theorem

Let \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) be irreducible of degree \(n\). Over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), it has exactly \(\gcd(n,m)\) distinct irreducible factors, each of degree \(n/\gcd(n,m)\).

Proof. Frobenius acts on the roots of \(f\) as an \(n\)-cycle. Over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), the relevant Frobenius is \(\sigma^m\). Its orbits have length \(n/\gcd(n,m)\), and each orbit is the root set of one irreducible factor.

Example

An irreducible polynomial of degree six over \(\mathbb F_2\) remains irreducible over \(\mathbb F_{32}\), splits into two cubics over \(\mathbb F_4\), and into three quadratics over \(\mathbb F_8\). It splits completely over \(\mathbb F_{64}\).

sections.title: Trace and norm
sections.body:
For \(\alpha\in\mathbb F_{q^n}\), \[\operatorname{Tr}_{q^n/q}(\alpha)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\alpha^{q^i},\qquad \operatorname{N}_{q^n/q}(\alpha)=\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}\alpha^{q^i}=\alpha^{(q^n-1)/(q-1)}.\] If \(\alpha\) has degree \(n\) and minimal polynomial \(x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0\), then \(a_{n-1}=-\operatorname{Tr}(\alpha)\) and \(a_0=(-1)^n\operatorname{N}(\alpha)\).

Thus prescribed trace and norm are prescribed coefficients. The other coefficients are elementary symmetric functions of the conjugates. Newton's identities relate these to the traces of powers, but division by an index divisible by the characteristic is unavailable. This is one reason that prescribed-coefficient arguments require care in small characteristic.

sections.title: Roots of unity
sections.body:
Suppose \(m>1\) and \(\gcd(m,q)=1\), and let \(\alpha\) have multiplicative order \(m\). Its degree over \(\mathbb F_q\) is the least \(d\ge1\) with \(q^d\equiv1\pmod m\), denoted by \(\operatorname{ord}_m(q)\). Hence the reduction of \(\Phi_m(x)\) is a product of \(\varphi(m)/\operatorname{ord}_m(q)\) distinct irreducibles of that degree.

Example

Since \(\operatorname{ord}_7(2)=3\), the seventh cyclotomic polynomial has two irreducible cubic factors over \(\mathbb F_2\): \[\Phi_7(x)=(x^3+x+1)(x^3+x^2+1).\] Both cubics have roots of multiplicative order seven.

If \(m=p^a u\) with \(p\nmid u\), then \(x^m-1=(x^u-1)^{p^a}\) in characteristic \(p\). Its distinct irreducible factors are therefore those of \(x^u-1\).

sections.title: From structure to construction
sections.body: The structural theory reduces finite-field irreducibility to Frobenius computations. Berlekamp's factorization algorithm and Rabin's irreducibility test made this viewpoint algorithmic. Later construction problems ask for more: few nonzero terms, prescribed coefficients, or roots that also generate a normal basis. These conditions lead to character sums, sieves, and questions about the distribution of irreducible polynomials.

title: Irreducibility over finite fields
subject: finite-fields
summary: Frobenius gives an exact irreducibility test, a counting formula, and a method for constructing irreducible polynomials.
questionsAnswered: How can irreducibility be tested without a complete factorization?
How many monic irreducible polynomials have a given degree?
How can an irreducible polynomial be constructed and checked?

sections.title: The Frobenius identity
sections.body:
For every \(m\ge1\), \[x^{q^m}-x=\prod_{\substack{P\text{ monic irreducible in }\mathbb F_q[x]\\ \deg P\mid m}}P(x).\] A root of an irreducible polynomial of degree \(d\) belongs to \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) exactly when \(d\mid m\). The derivative \(-1\) ensures that each factor occurs once.

This identity turns factor degrees into polynomial gcd computations. The required powers are computed modulo the polynomial under study; there is no need to write out \(x^{q^m}\).

sections.title: The irreducibility criterion
sections.body:
Theorem (Frobenius-power criterion)

A monic polynomial \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) of degree \(n\ge1\) is irreducible if and only if

\[x^{q^n}\equiv x\pmod f,\qquad \gcd\bigl(f,x^{q^{n/\ell}}-x\bigr)=1\quad\text{for every prime }\ell\mid n.\]

The first condition makes \(f\) squarefree and forces every factor degree to divide \(n\). If a proper divisor \(d\mid n\) occurred as a factor degree, some prime \(\ell\mid n/d\) would give \(d\mid n/\ell\), contradicting the corresponding gcd. The reverse implication follows from the same Frobenius identity. The criterion uses modular exponentiation and Euclidean gcds, without expanding the powers as polynomials.

citations.locator: Irreducibility testing over finite fields, Theorem 1
citations.note: Official documentation states the criterion and its exact algorithmic use.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

Take \(f=x^4+x+1\in\mathbb F_2[x]\). Repeated squaring modulo \(f\) gives

\[x^4\equiv x+1,\qquad x^8\equiv x^2+1,\qquad x^{16}\equiv x.\]

The only prime divisor of \(n=4\) is \(2\), and \(x^4-x\equiv1\pmod f\). Thus the required gcd is one, and \(f\) is irreducible. Its splitting field has 16 elements, and the Galois group over \(\mathbb F_2\) has order four.

The congruence \(x^{16}\equiv x\pmod f\) alone does not suffice: the reducible quartic \(x^4+x=x(x+1)(x^2+x+1)\) also divides \(x^{16}-x\). The gcd conditions eliminate smaller-degree factors.

citations.note: Application of the exact criterion; the displayed remainders are direct calculations.

sections.title: Counting irreducible polynomials
sections.body:
Let \(N_q(n)\) count monic irreducibles of degree \(n\) over \(\mathbb F_q\). Taking degrees in the Frobenius identity gives

Derivation

\[q^m=\sum_{d\mid m}dN_q(d),\qquad N_q(n)=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)q^{n/d}.\]

The second identity is Möbius inversion; \(\mu\) is the Möbius function. Bounding the proper-divisor terms by the geometric sum \(\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}q^j\le2q^{n/2}\) gives \(N_q(n)=q^n/n+O(q^{n/2}/n)\), uniformly for \(q\ge2\). Thus a uniform monic polynomial is irreducible with probability asymptotic to \(1/n\) as \(n\to\infty\), even for fixed \(q\).

Example

\[N_2(6)=\frac{64-8-4+2}{6}=9.\]

Thus nine of the 64 monic binary sextics are irreducible. All nine have constant coefficient one, so nine of the 32 constant-one sextics are irreducible.

sections.title: Construction algorithms
sections.body:
Choose independent uniform monic polynomials of degree \(n\), and apply the Frobenius test until one is irreducible. The output is always correct; only the running time is random. The expected number of trials is \(q^n/N_q(n)\), asymptotic to \(n\). For \(n\ge2\), sampling only nonzero constant coefficients reduces it to \((q-1)q^{n-1}/N_q(n)\). For binary sextics this is exactly \(32/9\).

If \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\) is already represented, choose \(\alpha\) outside every maximal proper subfield: \(\alpha^{q^{n/\ell}}\ne\alpha\) for each prime \(\ell\mid n\). Its minimal polynomial is \(\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(x-\alpha^{q^i})\), of degree \(n\).

Shoup develops deterministic construction algorithms and precise complexity bounds. The dependence on the characteristic matters: a bound polynomial in \(p\) is not necessarily polynomial in its bit length \(\log p\).

sections.title: Further conditions
sections.body:
An irreducible polynomial gives a field extension. Requiring its roots to generate the multiplicative group is an additional condition: such a polynomial is called primitive. Normality is another condition, concerning a basis of Frobenius conjugates. See primitive and normal elements.

Prescribing coefficients or requiring few nonzero terms restricts the candidates before the test is applied. Existence theorems for these restrictions are treated in coefficient restrictions and sparse polynomials.

sections.title: Parity of the number of factors
sections.body:
Let \(q\) be odd and let \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) be squarefree of degree \(n\), with \(r\) irreducible factors. Frobenius has \(r\) cycles on its roots, so its sign is \((-1)^{n-r}\). The discriminant is a square in \(\mathbb F_q^\times\) if and only if this sign is positive. Thus the discriminant determines the parity of \(r\), but usually not whether \(r=1\).

In characteristic two, every element of the ground field is a square. Swan's theorem instead uses a discriminant calculation after lifting to characteristic zero. It gives useful obstructions to irreducibility of binary trinomials; see the sparse-polynomial examples.

citations.note: The basic theorem is credited by Swan to Stickelberger, with Dalen’s prior proof noted.

title: Primitive and normal elements
subject: finite-fields
summary: A primitive element generates the multiplicative group. The conjugates of a normal element form a basis. Every finite-field extension contains an element with both properties.
status: Published theorems; preprint claim stated separately
questionsAnswered: What is the difference between a field generator, a primitive element, and a normal element?
How are primitivity and normality tested?
What is known about the Morgan–Mullen conjecture?

sections.title: Three properties of an element
sections.body:
Fix \(K=\mathbb F_{q^n}\) over \(\mathbb F_q\). An element \(\alpha\) is a field generator if \(K=\mathbb F_q(\alpha)\); equivalently, its minimal polynomial has degree \(n\). It is primitive if it generates \(K^\times\), and normal if \(\alpha,\alpha^q,\ldots,\alpha^{q^{n-1}}\) form an \(\mathbb F_q\)-basis of \(K\).

Primitivity and normality each imply degree \(n\), but degree \(n\) does not imply either of them. In \(\mathbb F_3(\alpha)\) with \(\alpha^2=-1\), the element \(\alpha\) has degree two and multiplicative order four; the full multiplicative group has order eight.

sections.title: Testing primitivity
sections.body:
Put \(N=q^n-1\). An element \(\alpha\in K^\times\) is primitive if and only if \[\alpha^{N/\ell}\ne1\quad\text{for every prime }\ell\mid N.\] Indeed, a proper divisor of \(N\) divides \(N/\ell\) for some prime \(\ell\mid N\). For an irreducible polynomial \(f\) of degree \(n\), these tests can be performed with \(\alpha=x\bmod f\).

The cyclic group \(K^\times\) has \(\varphi(N)\) generators. Frobenius groups them into orbits of length \(n\), so the number of monic primitive polynomials of degree \(n\) is \(\varphi(q^n-1)/n\).

citations.locator: Chapters 2–3, primitive elements and primitive polynomials

sections.title: Testing normality
sections.body:
Choose any \(\mathbb F_q\)-basis of \(K\). Form a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of \(\alpha,\alpha^q,\ldots,\alpha^{q^{n-1}}\). The element is normal exactly when this matrix has rank \(n\).

There is also a polynomial formulation. Let \(\sigma(\beta)=\beta^q\), and let \(m_\alpha(T)\) be the monic polynomial of least degree such that \(m_\alpha(\sigma)(\alpha)=0\). It divides \(T^n-1\). Normality is equivalent to \(m_\alpha(T)=T^n-1\), or to \[\bigl((T^n-1)/P(T)\bigr)(\sigma)(\alpha)\ne0\] for every distinct monic irreducible divisor \(P\) of \(T^n-1\). Here \(\sum b_iT^i\) acts as the linear map \(\beta\mapsto\sum b_i\beta^{q^i}\).

The criterion remains valid when the characteristic divides \(n\); the multiplicities in \(T^n-1\) must be retained.

citations.locator: §2, the polynomial module structure and freeness

sections.title: Examples
sections.body:
Example

Let \(\alpha\) be a root of \(x^3+x^2+1\) over \(\mathbb F_2\). The polynomial has no root in \(\mathbb F_2\), hence is irreducible. The nonzero element \(\alpha e1\) has order seven, so it is primitive. Also \(\alpha^4=\alpha^2+\alpha+1\). Relative to the basis \(1,\alpha,\alpha^2\), its conjugates have columns \((0,1,0)^t,(0,0,1)^t,(1,1,1)^t\), which are independent. Thus \(\alpha\) is normal.

In contrast, a root \( eta\) of \(x^4+x+1\) over \(\mathbb F_2\) is primitive but not normal. Irreducibility is checked in the quartic example; the tests \( eta^3 e1\) and \( eta^5= eta^2+ eta e1\) give order fifteen. Its trace is zero because the coefficient of \(x^3\) vanishes. Hence its four conjugates are linearly dependent.

citations.locator: Primitive elements, normal bases, and trace; the displayed examples are direct calculations.

sections.title: The primitive normal basis theorem
sections.body:
Theorem

For every prime power \(q\) and every \(n\ge1\), the extension \(\mathbb F_{q^n}/\mathbb F_q\) contains a primitive normal element.

Lenstra and Schoof proved this in 1987. Cohen and Huczynska later gave a proof without computer calculations. Their method counts elements satisfying multiplicative and additive conditions by character sums, then uses a sieve to show that the count is positive.

A stronger theorem asks for both \(\alpha\) and \(\alpha^{-1}\) to be normal over \(\mathbb F_q\), with \(\alpha\) primitive. Cohen and Huczynska proved that such an element exists except for \[(q,n)=(2,3),(2,4),(3,4),(4,3),(5,4).\] These five pairs are genuine exceptions.

sections.title: Counting normal elements
sections.body:
The normal basis theorem identifies \(K\), as an \(\mathbb F_q[T]\)-module with \(T\) acting by Frobenius, with \(\mathbb F_q[T]/(T^n-1)\). Its generators correspond to the units of this quotient. Therefore the number of normal elements is \[q^n\prod_{P\mid T^n-1}\left(1-q^{-\deg P}\right),\] where the product is over distinct monic irreducible factors.

For \(q=2,n=4\), one has \(T^4-1=(T+1)^4\), giving eight normal elements. In this case normality is equivalent to nonzero trace: \((\sigma-1)^3=1+\sigma+\sigma^2+\sigma^3\), and the normality test has just the factor \(P=T+1\).

citations.locator: §3, polynomial Euler function and normal elements

sections.title: Complete normality
sections.body:
An element of \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\) is completely normal over \(\mathbb F_q\) if it is normal over every intermediate field \(\mathbb F_{q^d}\), \(d\mid n\). Morgan and Mullen conjectured that every finite extension has an element that is both primitive and completely normal.

Write \(n=p^a m\), with \(p\nmid m\). A published theorem of Garefalakis and Kapetanakis proves existence when \(m

Preprint claim. Hellwig's October 2026 preprint claims existence for every \(q,n\). It combines a decomposition by partial Lagrange resolvents with character sums and finite computations. The author reports a Lean formalization for the new cases and computations, taking two earlier results as axioms and using Lean's compiler and interpreter for large computations.

questions.title: Does every finite extension have a primitive normal element?
questions.body: Yes. Lenstra and Schoof proved the primitive normal basis theorem; Cohen and Huczynska gave a later proof without computer calculations.

title: Factorization statistics over finite fields
subject: finite-fields
summary: Factor degrees follow permutation cycle statistics in several large-field limits. Exact counting explains the unrestricted case; monodromy and point counting handle suitable families.
questionsAnswered: How many polynomials have a specified list of factor degrees?
Why do permutations give the limiting proportions?
Which short intervals have the same factorization statistics?
How can a family have symmetric monodromy when individual splitting fields are cyclic?

sections.title: Factorization type
sections.body:
For a monic squarefree polynomial of degree \(n\), let \(m_j\) be the number of its irreducible factors of degree \(j\). Its factorization type is the partition \(\lambda=1^{m_1}2^{m_2}\cdots\), where \(\sum j m_j=n\). Frobenius acts on its roots with exactly these cycle lengths.

Put \(z_\lambda=\prod_{j\ge1}j^{m_j}m_j!\). A uniformly chosen permutation in \(S_n\) has cycle type \(\lambda\) with probability \(1/z_\lambda\): arrange the symbols into cycles, divide by rotations within each cycle, and divide by the order of cycles of equal length.

sections.title: Exact counting
sections.body:
Let \(N_q(j)\) be the number of monic irreducible polynomials of degree \(j\). Unique factorization gives the exact formula \[\#\{f\text{ monic squarefree of type }\lambda\}=\prod_{j\ge1}\binom{N_q(j)}{m_j}.\] For each degree, choose the required distinct irreducible factors; their product determines \(f\).

Since \(N_q(j)=q^j/j+O_j(q^{j/2})\), for fixed \(n\) this count is \(q^n/z_\lambda+O_n(q^{n-1})\) as \(q\to\infty\). Dividing by \(q^n\) gives the permutation probability in the limit. If repeated factors are allowed and their degrees are counted with multiplicity, the exact count instead uses \(\prod_j\binom{N_q(j)+m_j-1}{m_j}\).

citations.locator: Distribution of factorization patterns; the exact product is derived here.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
The three squarefree cubic types have counts \[\begin{array}{c|c|c}\text{type}&\text{count}&\text{limiting proportion}\\\hline 3&(q^3-q)/3&1/3\\2+1&q(q^2-q)/2&1/2\\1+1+1&\binom q3&1/6\end{array}\] Their sum is \(q^3-q^2\), the number of squarefree monic cubics.

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), the respective counts are \(2,2,0\). Thus the limiting proportions are not exact at a fixed small field. The lack of three distinct elements already excludes the third type.

citations.locator: Counting irreducibles and unique factorization; direct calculation.

sections.body:
Fix a monic \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) of degree \(n\), and let \[I(f,m)=\{f+h:h\in\mathbb F_q[x],\ \deg h\le m\},\qquad m

Theorem

For \(3\le m

The same estimate holds for \(m=1\) if the characteristic \(p\) does not divide \(n(n-1)\), and for \(m=2\) if \(p\ne2\) or \(\deg f'>1\).

sections.title: Monodromy and specialization
sections.body:
In a parameterized family, first compute the Galois group over the function field of the parameters. If the geometric group is \(S_n\), suitable finite-field point-counting estimates distribute the Frobenius classes according to their sizes in \(S_n\). A class with cycle type \(\lambda\) then contributes the proportion \(1/z_\lambda\).

This group belongs to the whole family. A particular polynomial over \(\mathbb F_q\) has a splitting field that is a finite field, whose Galois group is cyclic. Its Frobenius element contributes one cycle type to the family count. There is no claim that this individual polynomial has Galois group \(S_n\) over \(\mathbb F_q\).

sections.title: Restricted coefficient families
sections.body:
Entin gives a quantitative method for counting factorization types in restricted sets of specializations over large finite fields. Its usefulness depends on both the family's monodromy and an estimate measuring the restriction on the parameter set.

For example, coefficients uniform in the set of squares require additional arguments: the general error estimate need not give a useful bound. Bary-Soroker and Shmueli prove the irreducibility proportion \(1/n+O_n(q^{-1/2})\) in that model as \(q\to\infty\). See square coefficients for the precise probability model.

title: Sparse irreducible polynomials over finite fields
subject: finite-fields
summary: Sparse irreducibles give efficient finite-field representations. Their existence depends on the support, while sparse factors of cyclotomic polynomials form a separate classification problem.
questionsAnswered: Does every degree admit an irreducible polynomial with few nonzero terms?
How short can the lower-degree part of an irreducible polynomial be?
When are the irreducible factors of a cyclotomic polynomial sparse?

sections.title: Few nonzero coefficients
sections.body:
Let \(\sigma_q(n)\) be the least number of nonzero coefficients of an irreducible degree-\(n\) polynomial over \(\mathbb F_q\). Von zur Gathen–Nöcker conjecture, for \(n\ge2\),

\[\sigma_2(n)\le5,\qquad \sigma_q(n)\le4\quad(q\ge3).\]

These are existence statements: the support and coefficients may depend on the degree. They do not assert irreducibility for every polynomial of small weight.

The bounds also hold trivially in degree one, for example using \(x+1\). The equivalent binary formulation using trinomials or pentanomials concerns degrees at least two.

sections.title: A short lower-degree part
sections.body:
For \(n\ge2\), define \(\tau_q(n)=\min\{\deg h:x^n+h\text{ is irreducible over }\mathbb F_q,\ \deg h\[\tau_q(n)\le3+\log_q n.\]

The authors call these polynomials sedimentary. This condition bounds the positions of all nonleading terms, whereas sparsity bounds their number. Both forms allow fast reduction in a polynomial basis of \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\).

sections.title: Irreducible binomials
sections.body:
There is a complete criterion for the simplest support. Let \(a\in\mathbb F_q^\times\) have multiplicative order \(e\), and let \(n\ge2\). Then \(x^n-a\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb F_q\) if and only if every prime divisor of \(n\) divides \(e\) but does not divide \((q-1)/e\), and \(q\equiv1\pmod4\) whenever \(4\mid n\).

Example

Over \(\mathbb F_5\), the element \(2\) has order four. Hence \(x^{2^k}-2\) is irreducible for every \(k\ge1\). Over \(\mathbb F_3\), \(x^4+1\) fails the congruence condition and factors as \[(x^2+x+2)(x^2+2x+2).\]

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Over \(\mathbb F_2\), any polynomial with an even number of nonzero coefficients vanishes at \(1\). Thus an irreducible polynomial of degree greater than one must have odd weight. Swan’s theorem also excludes irreducible trinomials when \(8\mid n\). Five terms are therefore necessary in some degrees.

For degree eight,

\[x^8+x^4+x^3+x+1\]

is irreducible over \(\mathbb F_2\). Its exact Frobenius certificate is \(x^{256}\equiv x\pmod f\) and \(\gcd(f,x^{16}-x)=1\). The only prime divisor of eight is two, so these are precisely the required tests.

citations.note: Obstruction for binary trinomials in degrees divisible by eight.

sections.title: Sparse cyclotomic factors
sections.body:
A different problem asks whether every irreducible factor of \(x^m-1\), or of a single cyclotomic polynomial \(\Phi_m(x)\), has at most three nonzero terms. For \(m>1\) with \(\gcd(m,q)=1\), every irreducible factor of \(\Phi_m\) has degree \(\operatorname{ord}_m(q)\). Factors of \(x^m-1\) come from all \(\Phi_d\) with \(d\mid m\). The question is which coefficients of these factors vanish.

Oliveira and Reis classified the integers \(m\) for the \(x^m-1\) problem over \(\mathbb F_2\) and \(\mathbb F_4\). Cheng's characteristic-two extension has a published corrigendum and a corrected author version. The correction requires control of orders modulo powers of seven; the earlier implication from \(7\nmid q^2-1\) alone is insufficient. For example, \(\operatorname{ord}_{49}(128)=3\), and \(x^{49}-1\) over \(\mathbb F_{128}\) has an irreducible factor with four terms.

Correction to Theorem 1.3; arXiv:2507.10779v2, Proposition 3.4 and Example 5.2

sections.title: A single cyclotomic polynomial
sections.body:
Example

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), \[\Phi_{15}(x)=(x^4+x+1)(x^4+x^3+1),\] and both factors are irreducible trinomials. But \(\Phi_5(x)=x^4+x^3+x^2+x+1\) is irreducible because \(\operatorname{ord}_5(2)=4\). Thus every irreducible factor of \(\Phi_{15}\) is a trinomial, while \(x^{15}-1\) has a five-term irreducible factor.

Zhu and Wu's November 2026 preprint claims a classification of the pairs \((q,m)\), \(m>1\), \(\gcd(m,q)=1\), for which every irreducible factor of \(\Phi_m\) has exactly three nonzero terms. It reduces the supports by power substitutions and then studies root orders. This is a preprint result about individual cyclotomic polynomials; it does not settle the bounded-weight conjecture for every degree.

citations.locator: Theorem 2.47; the example follows by multiplication and Frobenius orders

sections.title: What the conjectures assert
sections.body:
The bounded-weight and short-tail conjectures above are recorded in von zur Gathen–Nöcker and the Handbook of Finite Fields. Their universal statements remain listed as open here; no resolution was verified in this review. A calculation proves existence only for the field and degree checked.

Once irreducibility of a degree-\(n\) polynomial over \(\mathbb F_q\) is established, its Galois group over \(\mathbb F_q\) is the cyclic group \(C_n\). The remaining difficulty is the prescribed shape of the polynomial.

questions.title: Does every binary degree admit an irreducible trinomial or pentanomial?
questions.scope: Every degree n≥2 over F_2; the support may depend on n.
questions.body: The conjecture is \(\sigma_2(n)\le5\). Even weights are impossible, and degrees divisible by eight require at least five terms.

questions.title: Do four nonzero terms suffice over every finite field with more than two elements?
questions.scope: Every prime power q≥3 and degree n≥2.
questions.body: The assertion is \(\sigma_q(n)\le4\). It asks for at least one irreducible polynomial in each degree, without fixing the positions or values of its coefficients.

questions.title: Can the lower-degree part always have degree at most \(3+\log_q n\)?
questions.scope: Every prime power q and degree n≥2.
questions.body: The question asks for an irreducible \(x^n+h\) with \(\deg h\le3+\log_q n\). The degree bound is logarithmic; the coefficients of \(h\) are free.

questions.title: When are all irreducible factors of a cyclotomic polynomial trinomials?
questions.scope: Prime powers \(q\), integers \(m>1\) with \(\gcd(m,q)=1\), and exactly three nonzero terms in every factor of \(\Phi_m\).
questions.body: Zhu and Wu claim a complete classification in arXiv:2611.00647v2 (November 2026). The condition concerns a single cyclotomic polynomial; it is stronger than asking for one sparse irreducible of its degree, and different from requiring all factors of \(x^m-1\) to be sparse.
